lead: The access matrix is a grid of the protection state. Each row is a domain, the rights a process holds now. Each column is an object such as a file or device. A cell lists the rights that domain has on that object: read, write, execute. One table makes every access question the same: does cell (D, F) contain the right? Real systems store only non-empty cells, as access lists or capability lists. The figure shows three domains and four objects.
prereq: You need: the domain as a row from 6.2 and the file object from Unit 5, File concept, attributes and access methods.

blocks.text: The matrix is M[D, O] ⊆ R. M is the access matrix, D a domain, O an object, R the set of rights. If read is in M[D1, F1], a process in D1 may read F1. An empty cell means no access. The full matrix has (number of domains) × (number of objects) cells. In the figure, D1 has r on F1, rw on F2, x on F4; D2 has r on F2, rw on F3; D3 has r on F1, rw on F4. The matrix is usually sparse: most cells are empty. Three special rights extend it. Copy (r*) lets a domain pass that right to another. Owner lets a domain add or remove rights in an object's column. Control lets a domain change another domain's row. These rights change the matrix itself.
Implementation stores only non-empty cells. Four standard schemes exist.

items: Authorization table (table of triples): keep triples (domain, object, rights) for non-empty cells only. Access is a search through the table, O(E), where E is the number of non-empty cells; no empty cells are stored.
Access list: one list per object, holding pairs (domain, rights). To check D, scan that object's list. Space is E entries plus O headers. Access time is proportional to entries on that object.

Capability list: one list per domain, holding pairs (object, rights). A process presents an entry; the kernel checks the list. Space is E entries plus D headers. Access time is proportional to entries in that domain.

Lock and key: each object keeps a short list of locks (bit patterns), one per right or per group of domains; each domain holds a set of keys. A domain may use an object if one of its keys matches one of that object's locks. This compresses the object side like an access list while keeping keys on the domain side like capabilities.

blocks.text: Compare on sparsity. If D = 1000 domains, O = 1000 objects, and E = 5000 non-empty cells, a dense matrix array needs 1,000,000 cells but gives O(1) lookup. Each list form needs 5000 entries plus headers. The saving is large. Access time trades off. A dense array is fastest. Access list is fast when an object is shared by few domains; capability is fast when a domain touches few objects. If one object is opened by every domain, its access list is long and the check is slow; a capability per domain is short. If one domain touches every object, its capability list is long; access lists stay short. Revocation differs: deleting a right from an object's access list is one edit, while finding every copied capability is hard. That is why access lists dominate general-purpose file systems and capabilities appear in tighter designs. This trade-off is the whole design question.

figure.caption: Cell (D1, F1) holds r, so a process in D1 may read F1 — one cell answers one access question. The five grey cells are empty, so a real store keeps only the seven non-empty ones, as access lists or capability lists.

spec.title: Access matrix: rows D1 to D3 are domains, columns F1 to F4 are objects
spec.aria: A three by four grid: domain D1 has read on object F1, read-write on F2 and execute on F4; D2 has read on F2 and read-write on F3; D3 has read on F1 and read-write on F4. The cell D1-F1 is highlighted to show one access question, and the five empty cells are shown grey against seven non-empty cells.

examples.question: Protection state: D1 has read on F1, read-write on F2, execute on F4. D2 has read on F2, read-write on F3. D3 has read on F1, read-write on F4. (a) Full matrix cells? (b) Non-empty cells? (c) Access-list entries? (d) Capability entries?
steps: Non-empty: D1 has 3, D2 2, D3 2, total 7.
An access list stores non-empty cells per object: 7 entries.
A capability list stores non-empty cells per domain: 7 entries.
examples.answer: 12 cells; 7 non-empty; access-list store 7; capability store 7.
examples.check:
domains = [["r", "rw", "-", "x"], ["-", "r", "rw", "-"], ["r", "-", "-", "rw"]]
cells = len(domains) * len(domains[0])
non_empty = sum(1 for row in domains for c in row if c != "-")
access_list = non_empty
capability = sum(1 for row in domains for c in row if c != "-")
print(cells)
print(non_empty)
print(access_list)
print(capability)

traps: Storing the whole matrix as a dense array; it is sparse and wastes space.
Swapping rows and columns: access lists are per object; capability lists are per domain.
Confusing copy and control: copy passes one right; control changes another domain's row.
Assuming both forms store different totals: both store E non-empty entries; headers differ.

quiz.q: In the access matrix, what is a row and what is a column?
quiz.a: A row is a domain; a column is an object; a cell lists the rights.

quiz.q: Why do real systems not store the full matrix?
quiz.a: It is sparse; a full array wastes space on empty cells.

quiz.q: A matrix has 5 domains, 8 objects, and 13 non-empty cells. How many entries does an access-list store hold? A capability store?
quiz.a: Both hold 13 entries; headers are 8 object lists versus 5 domain lists.

quiz.q: One file is opened by 500 domains. Which lookup is longer: access list or capability list? Why?
quiz.a: Access list: it scans 500 entries for that file; each capability list stays short.

quiz.q: D1 has rw on F1 and r on F2; D2 has r on F1. Give the access list for F1 and the capability list for D1.
Why is revocation easier with access lists than with capabilities?
quiz.a: Removing a right edits one object list; capability copies may be in many domains.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern kernels mix both forms: Linux checks mode bits and ACLs on inodes, while Windows uses security descriptors with access-control lists. Capability ideas appear in microkernels and in unforgeable file descriptors. Search for 'access control list', 'capability-based security', and 'protection matrix' to go further.
